lesson.menu_desc: Feedback vocabulary + hedging with modals: might, could, would suggest, it seems -- 27 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 22 -- Hedging & Softening Language
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Eduarda | Lesson 22 -- Hedging & Softening Language

listenings.text: Hi Eduarda, it's James. Quick thought before you meet the client tomorrow. Their CEO built the business plan himself, so he will take any criticism personally. Don't be blunt, but don't sugarcoat it either. The revenue forecast is too high, and he needs to hear that. Start with what works, then add your caveat. Say something like: it seems that the growth rate might be a little optimistic. And give him a way forward: I would suggest a second scenario with lower growth. If he has reservations, listen first. Our job is to be honest and still keep the client. Call me after the meeting.

In business, the same message can sound helpful or rude. The difference is often a few small words. This is called hedging. Instead of saying the numbers are wrong, say the numbers might need another look. Instead of you must change this, say I would suggest changing this. Words like seems, might, could, slightly and a bit make your message softer, but they do not change the facts. Be careful, though. Too much hedging and your message disappears. One or two softeners per sentence is enough. Your opinion should still be clear at the end.

extra_audio.text: Eduarda opened Ryan's model the night before the client meeting. She saw that the revenue forecast was too high. Instead of being blunt, she started with what worked in the model. Then she added a caveat: the growth rate might be a little optimistic. She suggested a second scenario with lower growth. Ryan took the feedback well and updated the model before the meeting.
